front: What is the difference between a program and a process?
back: A program is a file on disk, for example `/usr/bin/ls`. A process is a running instance of it with its own PID. One program can have many processes.

front: Where do system-wide configuration files live, and where do logs and changing data live?
back: Configuration is in `/etc/` (plain text, edited as root), and logs and changing data are under `/var`, for example `/var/log/`.

front: Where are settings that affect only one user stored?
back: In hidden files (names starting with a dot) in that user’s home directory.

front: What is PID 1?
back: The first process the kernel starts. It starts all the others, so every process has a parent. On most modern distributions it is `systemd`.

front: What does `ps` show without options, and what do `ps -e` and `ps -ef` show?
back: Without options only your processes in the current terminal. `ps -e` shows every process, and `ps -ef` shows every process in the full format with PID and parent PID.

front: What is the difference between `ps -ef` and `ps aux`?
back: Both show every process. `ps -ef` is the System V style with PPID and start time; `ps aux` is the BSD style (no dash) with `%CPU` and `%MEM`.

front: What is the difference between `ps` and `top`?
back: `ps` is a snapshot, printed once. `top` is a live view that redraws every few seconds, sorted by CPU use, and shows the load average. Press `q` to quit.

front: In `top`, what do the keys `q`, `k` and `M` do?
back: `q` quits, `k` kills a process (it asks for the PID) and `M` sorts by memory. `P` sorts by CPU.

front: Which command shows memory and swap, and what do `free -h` and the `available` column mean?
back: `free`. `-h` prints human-readable sizes. `available` estimates what programs could use now; it is a better guide than `free`, which is often low because Linux uses spare RAM as cache.

front: What is swap?
back: Disk space the kernel uses as spare memory when RAM runs out. It is much slower than RAM.

front: What is `/proc`?
back: A pseudo-filesystem made up by the kernel while the system runs. Each process has a numbered directory such as `/proc/1`, and files like `/proc/cpuinfo` and `/proc/meminfo` hold system facts.

front: Which command starts, stops and checks the service `buildd` on a systemd system?
back: `sudo systemctl start buildd`, `sudo systemctl stop buildd` and `systemctl status buildd`. Changing a service needs root.

front: What does the `Active:` line of `systemctl status` tell you?
back: The service’s state, such as `active (running)`, `inactive (dead)` or `failed`, and since when. The `Loaded:` line says where the unit file is and whether it is enabled.

front: What is the difference between `systemctl start` and `systemctl enable`?
back: `start` runs the service now, and `enable` makes it start at every boot. `start` alone does not survive a reboot.

front: Why can’t you read the systemd journal with `cat` or `grep`, and what do you use?
back: The journal is stored in a binary format, not plain text. Use `journalctl` to read it.

front: What do `journalctl -u ssh` and `journalctl -b` show?
back: `-u ssh` shows only messages of the `ssh` unit (service), and `-b` only messages since the current boot.

front: Which `journalctl` options show the last 20 lines, follow new messages and filter by priority?
back: `journalctl -n 20` shows the last 20 lines, `-f` follows new messages like `tail -f`, and `-p err` shows errors and more serious ones.

front: What does `dmesg` print?
back: The kernel’s ring buffer: hardware found at boot, driver loading, USB devices plugged in and disk errors. It may need root. `journalctl -k` shows the same kernel messages.

front: What is a ring buffer?
back: A block of memory of fixed size where new lines overwrite the oldest. The kernel uses one for its messages, which `dmesg` prints.

front: Which directory holds plain-text log files, and which tools work on them?
back: `/var/log/`. Because the files are text, `less`, `tail -f` and `grep` work. Typical files are `syslog`, `auth.log` and `dpkg.log` on Debian-based systems.

front: Which log file records logins and `sudo` use on Debian-based systems?
back: `/var/log/auth.log`. Some files in `/var/log` can be read only by root.

front: What does logrotate do?
back: It renames old log files (`syslog.1`, `syslog.2.gz`) and starts new ones, so logs don’t grow forever.

front: What is a memory address, and what does a process see?
back: Every byte of RAM has a number, its address. The kernel gives each process its own virtual address space, so processes can’t read or overwrite each other’s memory.

front: In which file can you see the address ranges of a process, and in what notation?
back: `/proc/<PID>/maps`. The addresses are written in hexadecimal, such as `7f3c2a000000`.

front: What does the syslog service do with a message?
back: It sorts messages by facility (who sent it, such as `auth` or `kern`) and priority (how serious) and writes them to files in `/var/log/`, as set in `/etc/rsyslog.conf`.

front: Name the syslog priorities from least to most serious.
back: `debug`, `info`, `notice`, `warning`, `err`, `crit`, `alert`, `emerg`.

front: Which file normally holds kernel messages, and what are the older exam’s directories to know?
back: `/var/log/kern.log` holds kernel messages. `/etc/` has configuration, `/var/log/` logs, `/boot/` the kernel, `/proc/` process info, `/dev/` devices and `/sys/` devices and drivers.

front: Which log files hold general and authentication messages, depending on the distribution?
back: General messages go to `/var/log/syslog` or `/var/log/messages`, and authentication messages to `/var/log/auth.log` or `/var/log/secure`. Kernel messages also reach syslog.
